title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
prompt: You are given an integer `k` and an array `prices` where `prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. Find the maximum profit achievable with at most `k` transactions (a transaction is one buy followed by one sell). You must sell the stock before you buy again.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 0 (price=2), sell on day 1 (price=4), profit=2. A second transaction isn't profitable.
Buy on day 1 (price=2), sell on day 2 (price=6), profit=4. Buy on day 4 (price=0), sell on day 5 (price=3), profit=3. Total=7.
With k=0 transactions allowed, no trade can be made no matter how the prices move, so the profit is always 0.

hints: This generalizes the 'at most 2 transactions' version: instead of 4 fixed rolling variables, you need 2*k of them, one buy/sell pair per allowed transaction.

If k is very large (>= prices.length / 2), the transaction limit is not actually binding — you can treat it like the unlimited-transactions version and just sum every profitable adjacent price increase, which is much cheaper than the general DP.

Otherwise, maintain buy[1..k] and sell[1..k] arrays. For each day's price, update buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t-1] - price) and sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + price) for t from 1 to k, using sell[0] = 0 as the base.

solution.approach: Generalize the fixed-two-transaction rolling-variable trick to k transactions. Maintain buy[t] and sell[t] for t = 1..k, where buy[t] is the best net profit after the t-th purchase and sell[t] is the best profit after the t-th sale. Initialize every buy[t] to -infinity and sell[t] to 0. For each day's price, update t from 1 to k in increasing order: buy[t] = max(buy[t], sell[t-1] - price) (start the t-th transaction by reinvesting profit from the (t-1)-th) and sell[t] = max(sell[t], buy[t] + price) (close the t-th transaction today). As a critical optimization, if k >= len(prices) // 2, the transaction cap can never actually bind (you can't complete more than len(prices)//2 disjoint transactions anyway), so the problem degenerates to the unlimited-transactions case: just sum every positive day-over-day price increase, which is O(n) instead of O(n*k). The final answer is sell[k] in the general case.
solution.timeComplexity: O(n * k) in general, O(n) when k is large enough to be non-binding
